comparison: Both address the core dataset and TE polymorphism calls (C3, C4, C7, C8, C9). OpenEval finds the data well-supported with appropriate validation, while peer reviewers express uncertainty due to concerns about false positive rates in the TE calling pipeline and relatively low coverage thresholds that could affect data quality.

Both address demographic history and sample composition (C1, C2, C52, C53). OpenEval finds these claims well-supported by prior citations, and peer reviewers accept this background without challenge, treating it as established context from prior publications.

Both address age-adjusted SFS analyses showing purifying selection (C18, C19, C20, C21). OpenEval finds the evidence well-supported with appropriate statistical testing. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, with Reviewer 1 raising concerns that the signal far from genes may be a mapping quality artifact rather than biological signal, despite statistical significance.

Both address SFS analysis showing shift toward rare alleles (C17). OpenEval finds this supported and consistent with purifying selection. Peer reviewers express uncertainty about related claims, particularly questioning whether signals far from genes represent true biological effects or technical artifacts.

Both address age-adjusted SFS for DNA-transposons (C22). OpenEval finds the differential effects between TE types interesting and supported. Peer reviewers' uncertainty about the broader SFS findings (particularly the artifact concerns) may extend to this claim as well.

Both address forward simulations estimating neutral TE proportions (C23, C49). OpenEval finds the simulations appropriately designed though notes assumptions about parameters. Peer reviewers support these findings, with the editor and reviewers affirming that purifying selection is the main force, though Reviewer 1 notes most conclusions rely on the 10% of polymorphisms from retrotransposons.

Both address selection coefficient estimation from age distributions (C24, C50). OpenEval finds the approach reasonable with sensitivity analyses strengthening conclusions. Peer reviewers support these findings, with Reviewer 2 specifically praising the age-adjustment approach as an interesting way to reduce bias.

Both address Mantel test results on TE-population structure correlations (C5, C6). OpenEval finds the statistical results well-supported though cautions about causal interpretation. Peer reviewers accept these demographic and population structure findings without challenge as part of the overall evidence base.

Both address correlations with effective population size (C43, C44). OpenEval finds the negative correlation with Ne consistent with efficient purifying selection in larger populations. Peer reviewers accept these findings as supporting evidence for broader conclusions about selection.

Both address ANCOVA results on iHS and TE age (C10, C11, C12). OpenEval finds the lack of iHS effect well-supported, suggesting TEs are not enriched in regions under recent positive selection. Peer reviewers strongly support this finding as part of the broader conclusion that positive selection on TEs is rare, with all three reviewers affirming the evidence.

Both address XtX analysis of population differentiation (C13, C14). OpenEval finds the very small proportion of over-differentiated TEs provides strong evidence against widespread positive selection. Peer reviewers strongly support this as part of the convincing evidence that positive selection on TE polymorphisms is rare.

Both address GEA results on environmentally-associated TEs (C15, C16). OpenEval finds the extremely low proportion strongly supports limited TE contribution to adaptation. Peer reviewers strongly support this finding, with the editor and reviewers affirming only a few putatively adaptive variants were detected.

Both address the main conclusion about rare positive selection (C48, C51). OpenEval finds the convergence of evidence from multiple methods strengthens these conclusions. Peer reviewers strongly support this, with all three reviewers explicitly affirming the finding that positive selection on TE polymorphisms is rare and the evidence is convincing.

Both address the overarching conclusion about TE evolution and adaptation (C51). OpenEval finds the conclusion well-supported by convergent evidence from multiple analyses. Peer reviewers strongly support this, with the editor noting the study's relevance for understanding TEs in evolution and Reviewer 1 stating it makes an important addition to knowledge of TE dynamics.

OpenEval finds background claims about B. distachyon biology (C25-C29, C31-C34) well-supported by appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though reviewers implicitly accept this background context.

OpenEval finds general background claims on TE biology (C35-C42) well-supported by appropriate literature citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers focus on novel findings rather than established background.

OpenEval finds claims about TE effects on gene expression (C45-C47) appropriately cited from prior work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though this background supports interpretation of distance-dependent selection effects.

OpenEval finds methodological decisions about treating TEs as homozygous and mutation rates (C54, C55, C57) reasonable and well-justified. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though these assumptions underlie analyses that reviewers do evaluate.
